plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single three-dimensional diagram of a closed surface carrying outward normal vectors. A pale blue solid shaped like a rectangular prism with bulging faces and rounded edges occupies the center, set in a frame whose z axis rises at the upper left, y axis extends right, and x axis comes forward to the lower left. The letter E labels the solid at its middle and the letter S labels the boundary near its upper right. Short dark blue arrows, each labeled N, project outward from the boundary: two from the top, two from the bottom, one from the left face, one from the right face, and one drawn on the upper surface angling up and back. Longer unlabeled orange arrows run in parallel through and around the figure from lower left to upper right, standing for the ambient vector field. Dashed curves mark the hidden rear edges. Setting the labeled normals against the uniformly directed field arrows shows at a glance how much of the field crosses the boundary at each face. The diagram accompanies a result tying the flux of a vector field across a closed surface to a triple integral of its divergence over the solid inside.

elements: pale blue closed solid E shaped like a rectangular prism with slightly bulging faces and rounded edges
label E at the center of the solid
label S near the upper-right edge of the boundary surface
seven outward normal arrows N (dark blue): two from the top face, two from the bottom face, one from the left face, one from the right face, one on the upper surface angled up and back
ambient vector field: roughly six longer parallel orange arrows running from lower-left to upper-right, passing through and around the solid
dashed curves marking the hidden rear edges of the solid
z axis vertical at upper left with arrowhead and label z
y axis extending to the right with arrowhead and label y
x axis coming forward to the lower left with arrowhead and label x

interactions.teaches: Selecting a face of S brightens its outward normal and the nearby field arrows, showing whether the field crosses that patch mostly outward (positive flux), mostly inward (negative flux), or skims along it (little flux)

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: Switching from arrows crossing S to a translucent volume emphasis inside E shows that the divergence theorem equates total flux through the boundary with divergence accumulated throughout the enclosed solid

demo_steps.title: Right face: positive flux
demo_steps.narration: Click the right face. Its normal points with the orange field, so the field flows out of S here — positive flux contribution.

demo_steps.title: Left face: negative flux
demo_steps.narration: Click the left face. The field enters the solid against the outward normal here — a negative flux contribution.

demo_steps.title: Volume view
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the enclosed-volume view. Shading fills E to suggest the divergence accumulating inside; the net of all the signed face contributions equals this interior accumulation.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Solid E: rounded box ~5 (X, depth) × 4.5 (Y, screen-right) × 2.2 (Z, up) world units centered at origin, faces gently bulged outward and edges rounded; pale translucent blue #a9c4dd with slightly darker edge lines. Label E at its center, S just outside the upper-right edge. Field arrows: ~6 orange #e8862e arrows, all parallel, direction roughly (+0.5, +0.85, +0.1) normalized, length ~2.5 units, spaced across the solid so some pass through it and some pass beside it. Normals N: dark blue #1f4e9c arrows ~0.8 units long placed as in the source: two on top pointing +Z, two on bottom pointing -Z, one on left face pointing -Y, one on right face pointing +Y, one on the upper surface tilted up and toward -X/back. Dashed dark-blue curves along the hidden rear-bottom and rear-left edges. Axes: z up at the left rear corner, y to the right, x diagonally down-left toward viewer, each extending ~3 units beyond the solid, thin black lines with arrowheads and italic labels.
interactionPlan.notes: Render the solid with a semi-transparent MeshPhysicalMaterial so field arrows passing through remain visible; draw field arrows with depthTest on but render after the solid. For face selection, raycast against the six face regions (use invisible plane proxies per face); brighten the selected face's normals and the two nearest field arrows while dimming others. In Enclosed-volume view, fade the field arrows to 30% opacity and raise the solid's interior emissive/opacity slightly to suggest accumulation inside E. Keep axis lines and labels as screen-space-anchored sprites so they stay legible.

authoredContext:
Let S be a piecewise, smooth closed surface that encloses solid E in space. Assume that S is oriented outward, and let F be a vector field with continuous partial derivatives on an open region containing E (the figure). Then

The divergence theorem follows the general pattern of these other theorems. If we think of divergence as a derivative of sorts, then the divergence theorem relates a triple integral of derivative divF over a solid to a flux integral of F over the boundary of the solid. More specifically, the divergence theorem relates a flux integral of vector field F over a closed surface S to a triple integral of the divergence of F over the solid enclosed by S.

The divergence theorem relates a flux integral across a closed surface S to a triple integral over solid E enclosed by the surface.

A diagram of a closed surface S, vector field, and solid E enclosed by the surface in three dimensions. The surface is a roughly rectangular prism with curved sides. The normal vectors stretch out and away from the surface. The arrows have negative x components and positive y and z components.

Recall that the flux form of Green’s theorem states that ∬DdivFdA=∫CF·Nds. Therefore, the divergence theorem is a version of Green’s theorem in one higher dimension.

Add one or two more rim normals (including a horizontal side normal) to match the source's distribution of N arrows
